title: What Have You Heard?
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart takes on a quiet failure in lesson-observation feedback: the observer and the teacher leave the same meeting believing they agreed, then act on different understandings. He diagnoses three causes - mental models that filter what each person hears, shared jargon that invites each side to fill gaps with assumptions, and emotion that edits the message in real time. His remedy is a single question, 'What have you heard?', which asks the teacher to restate the takeaway in their own words, exposing interpretation rather than recall, turning a broadcast into a conversation, and giving the teacher permission to clarify. He then steps back to co-observation, arguing that two observers must first ask each other 'What did you notice?' so they calibrate before meeting the teacher. The piece ends on design: the check only works if the meeting protects time for it, producing a slower, more provisional conversation in which the next step is co-constructed rather than delivered.
points: Hart's sharpest line is that a smooth feedback conversation is not evidence of understanding, only evidence that no one has yet tested it.
Asking the teacher to restate the feedback in their own words reveals the sense they made of it, which is where observer intention and teacher understanding usually diverge.
The question also legitimises clarification for teachers who would otherwise leave with unanswered questions to avoid appearing uncertain.
With co-observers, calibration comes first: 'What did you notice?' between observers prevents two leaders pulling the feedback meeting in subtly different directions.
The practice fails if bolted on as a thirty-second closing question; the meeting must be designed with pauses and provisional thinking so the next step is co-constructed.
quotes: Teaching is complex, the giving and receiving of feedback is emotional work, and everyone brings their own mental models to the table. The result is predictable: conversations that feel aligned in the moment diverge as soon as people walk out of the room. And when that happens, the work that follows is incoherent at best.

These phrases feel clear to the person saying them, but the person hearing them has to infer the detail. Because the conversation felt smooth, we assume alignment. But a smooth conversation is not evidence of understanding; it’s evidence that no one has yet tested it.

Even the most constructive feedback can activate pride, defensiveness or uncertainty. When that happens, the brain starts filtering, softening, amplifying or discarding parts of the message without conscious thought.

It reveals the interpretation of your feedback. When a teacher explains what they have heard, you see the sense they have made of it, not just whether they can repeat your phrasing. This is often where the surprises lie; the places where your intention and their understanding diverge.

It legitimises clarification. Teachers might sometimes leave feedback conversations with unanswered questions because they do not want to appear uncertain. Making interpretation explicit gives them permission to ask, refine and check.

These short exchanges create calibration. They reveal where observers agree, where they differ, and which parts of the lesson truly matter for the feedback conversation ahead. Without this step, two observers can walk into a feedback meeting believing they are aligned, only to pull the conversation in subtly different directions.

When this becomes habit, feedback meetings feel calmer and more deliberate. The message is clearer because it has been co-constructed, not delivered. The next step is understood because both people had time to test it, shape it and recognise its purpose.
